Maryland Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession FAQ

Can a squatter take ownership of my Maryland house?

Check the statute and talk to a Maryland attorney about your facts.

Can a squatter take ownership of a Maryland house?

Only after meeting every element of adverse possession for 20 years, and a court has to agree. A person who simply moves into a vacant house has no ownership claim the day they arrive.

The 20 year number comes from Courts and Judicial Proceedings 5-103(a). It gives a person 20 years from the date the cause of action accrues either to file suit to recover possession of land or to enter the land. After that window the true owner's right to recover is cut off. The statute leaves the common-law doctrine of prescription alone for rights such as easements, and it preserves the limits in Real Property 6-103 and 8-107.

For an owner, the practical meaning is that years of absence create the exposure. A vacant inherited house, a rental left empty after a tenant moved out, or a lot nobody has walked in years are the situations where a claim could grow over time.

What does a claimant have to prove?

Maryland courts describe three elements: possession that is actual, open, notorious and exclusive; possession that is continuous for the full period; and possession that is hostile and under a claim of title or ownership. Maryland appellate opinions quote this three-part test from Senez v. Collins.

An unreported 2022 opinion on the Maryland Courts site repeats that the claimant carries the burden of showing the elements for 20 years. It also quotes Hungerford v. Hungerford: every element must be shown, and if one is missing the possession does not give title.

ElementWhat it means for a house
Actual, open, notorious, exclusiveLiving in or openly using the house in a way the owner could see, without sharing control with the owner
Continuous for 20 yearsNo long gaps in use during the period
Hostile, under claim of titleOccupying as if the owner, not with the owner's permission

Permission matters. Someone who stays with the owner's consent, or under a lease, is not hostile in the legal sense, which is one reason a written record of who was allowed in can help an owner later.

How do I remove someone from my Maryland property?

The route depends on who the person is. A current or former tenant goes through the landlord-tenant process, while someone with no lease and no right to be there can be removed through a wrongful detainer case or, since October 2025, a sheriff affidavit for fraudulent occupancy.

For tenants and holdovers, the Maryland Courts housing page states the sequence: the landlord first wins a judgment in a rent court, breach of lease or holding over case, then petitions for a warrant of restitution. A sheriff or constable must be present at the eviction, and it cannot happen on a Sunday or a holiday. Owners cannot lock out an occupant on their own.

For an unauthorized occupant who is not a tenant, the wrongful detainer action in Real Property 14-132 applies. People's Law Library describes it as a District Court case for someone holding possession without the right to it. It cannot be used against a current tenant, a holdover tenant or someone with a court order protecting their possession.

  • Lease or rent history exists: use the landlord-tenant case and a warrant of restitution.
  • No lease and no permission: consider wrongful detainer.
  • Unsure of the occupant's status: ask a Maryland attorney before acting.

What changed for squatters in Maryland in 2025?

Senate Bill 46 (Chapter 188 of the 2025 laws) took effect October 1, 2025. It created a new crime of fraudulent occupancy and sped up the wrongful detainer process.

Under the new Criminal Law 8-906, it is a misdemeanor to occupy or claim a right to occupy a residence you have no lawful right to, with intent to defraud. A first violation carries up to 90 days in jail, a fine up to $500, or both. A second violation within two years rises to up to six months and $1,000, and later violations within two years of the previous one go up to one year and $2,500.

An owner can file a sworn affidavit with the county sheriff saying a person is fraudulently in possession. The sheriff must then remove that person and return the property, but a deputy may not remove an occupant who shows evidence of lawful possession. The offense does not apply where a court order granted possession or where a remedy exists under Title 8 of the Real Property Article, so landlord-tenant disputes stay in court.

How fast is a wrongful detainer case now?

Faster than before. The same 2025 act, Chapter 188, set tight deadlines for each step.

StepRule in Chapter 188
SummonsMay be addressed to OCCUPANT LOCATED AT the property address when the name is unknown
HearingNo more than 10 business days after the complaint is filed
ServiceCompleted within 4 business days; after two good-faith attempts on different days, mailing plus posting counts
DefaultCourt must enter a default judgment if the defendant does not attend
AppealDeadline cut from 10 days to 4 days after judgment

The owner still has to show a legal interest in the property. If the court finds the owner entitled to possession, it issues a warrant directing the sheriff to deliver possession immediately. Damages and fees may be awarded if they were claimed in the complaint. Note that older guides, including some still online, list a 10 day appeal period that no longer applies.

How can an adverse possession claim affect selling a house?

A claim, or even a rumor of one, clouds title and can stall a closing. Buyers and their title companies will ask who occupies the property and on what basis.

Real Property 14-108 lets a person in peaceable possession, under color of title or claim of right, bring a quiet title action in the circuit court where the land sits. The adverse claim does not have to be actively asserted. A suit of this kind must name anyone who appears of record or who claims a hostile outstanding right. For an owner, that means an old boundary dispute or an occupant's claim of ownership can end up before a judge before a clean sale is possible.

Cash Home Buyers works with Maryland sellers who have occupied, inherited or neglected houses, and we buy as-is. If someone is living in a house you own, your first step is to find out whether they are a tenant, a guest or an unauthorized occupant, because that decides which court process applies.

  • Keep copies of leases, texts and receipts that show whether the occupant had permission.
  • Photograph the property and record the dates you last inspected it.
  • Pay taxes and keep insurance active on a vacant house.
  • Do not change locks or remove belongings before a court order.

What should owners of vacant Maryland houses do?

Visit the property regularly, keep records of those visits and act quickly when someone is in the house without permission.

Bills in the legislature show the topic is moving. A 2025 fiscal note for Senate Bill 989 describes a proposed sheriff registry of unauthorized occupants for owners of residential dwellings, with enrollment for six months. The fiscal note is for the bill as introduced, and we could not confirm that it became law, so check the General Assembly site for current status before relying on it.

More questions about Maryland Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession

How long does adverse possession take in Maryland?

The statute sets 20 years from when the owner's cause of action accrues. Courts also require the possession to be continuous and hostile for that full period.

Is a squatter the same as a tenant in Maryland?

No. A tenant has a lease or rental agreement and the owner removes a tenant through the landlord-tenant court process and a warrant of restitution. An unauthorized occupant with no lease can be the subject of a wrongful detainer case.

Can the sheriff remove a squatter in Maryland?

Yes in some cases. Since October 1, 2025, an owner can file a sworn affidavit of fraudulent occupancy with the county sheriff, but the sheriff may not remove someone who shows evidence of lawful possession.

How fast is wrongful detainer in Maryland?

The hearing must be no more than 10 business days after the complaint is filed, and service must be completed within 4 business days. The appeal deadline is now 4 days.

Can I change the locks on someone living in my house?

Do not. For tenants, Maryland Courts says eviction needs a court judgment and a warrant of restitution carried out with the sheriff or constable present.

Maryland statutes set the basic rules between landlords and tenants, including deposits, notices and what happens when a rental is sold.

What the official sources say

  • A landlord may not impose a security deposit in excess of the equivalent of 1 month's rent per dwelling unit, regardless of the number of tenants; a landlord who overcharges is liable for up to three times the extra amount plus attorney's fees. (Md. Code, Real Property § 8-203(b)(1), (b)(3); source)
  • Within 45 days after the tenancy ends, the landlord must return the deposit with simple interest (greater of the daily U.S. Treasury yield curve rate for 1 year or 1.5% a year), less damages rightfully withheld. (Real Property § 8-203(e)(1); source)
  • If any deposit is withheld, the landlord must mail an itemized list of damages and costs within 45 days after the tenancy ends or forfeits the right to withhold for damages; wrongful failure to return can cost up to threefold plus attorney's fees. (Real Property § 8-203(e)(4), (g); source)
  • For a written lease for a term over 1 week or a month-to-month tenancy, notice to terminate is 60 days before expiration of the tenancy; year-to-year is 90 days; week-to-week is 7 days (written lease) or 21 days (no written lease). (Real Property § 8-402(b)-(c); source)
  • A tenant may use rent escrow (paying rent to a third party/court) where the landlord fails to fix defects after notice; the tenant must first notify the landlord of defects and request repairs. (Housing Cases (Maryland Courts); source)

Maryland law requires a landlord to give a specific written notice before filing an eviction, and the number of days depends on the reason.

What the official sources say

  • Before filing a failure-to-pay-rent case, landlord must give the tenant written notice of intent to file, giving 10 days to cure, on a Judiciary-created form (DC-CV-115); the complaint must state the date notice was given. (Real Property § 8-401(c); source)
  • Nonpayment cases are filed in the District Court; the judgment orders possession within 4 days after trial (extendable up to 15 days with a physician certificate); if the tenant tenders rent, late fees and costs at trial, the complaint is satisfied. (Real Property § 8-401; source)
  • If the tenant does not comply within 7 days of a landlord judgment, the court issues a warrant of restitution to a county official, who may remove the tenant's goods. (Real Property § 8-401(f)(1); source)
  • Breach of lease: landlord must give 30 days' written notice that the tenant is in violation and the landlord wants to repossess (one of the alternatives in the section). (Real Property § 8-402.1; source)
  • No-cause/end of term: 60 days' notice for month-to-month tenancy or a written term lease over 1 week; 90 days for year-to-year. (Real Property § 8-402; source)
  • Landlord must notify tenant of the eviction date at least 6 days before eviction (mail with certificate of mailing, post on property, and send electronically if email/cell known); the sheriff or constable carries out the eviction. (Housing Cases (Maryland Courts); Real Property § 8-407; source)
